power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading condition examined using network analysis.
However, meta-analytic evidence is limited for Major depressive disorder (MDD) symptom network studies.

Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses reporting guidelines, we searched Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL and bibliographies of previous literature for articles that have produced MDD symptom networks.
After screening, 153 articles (N = 1,580,674) were included in this review, consisting of 130 cross-sectional and 23 temporal network analysis studies.
A random-effects Meta-analytic Gaussian Network Aggregation (MAGNA) of MDD symptom networks was estimated based on available data.
Despite a pronounced variation in MDD measures and sample demographics, findings consistently showed that depressed mood emerged as the most central symptom.

Collectively, this systematic review and meta-analysis underscores network analysis as a technique for understanding MDD symptom dynamics and one that has the potential to improve psychological interventions.
Ongoing efforts toward intensive longitudinal datasets and improved reporting practices represent two key avenues for MDD network analysis research.
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is comprised of multiple symptoms that can be expressed differentially (Athira et al., 2020; Jermy et al., 2021).

text.text: According to the fifth edition of the

Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022), to reach the diagnostic threshold for MDD an individual must report experiencing at least five of nine symptoms, including either depressed mood or anhedonia over the same two-week period.

These nine symptoms include: 1) depressed mood; 2) anhedonia; 3) loss or increase in appetite; 4) insomnia or hypersomnia; 5) psychomotor agitation; 6) fatigue; 7) feelings of worthlessness; 8) impaired concentration; and 9) suicidal ideation.
A body of research has demonstrated that this categorisation of MDD has produced a high degree of variation in presentation (Buch & Conor, 2021; Goldberg 2011; Lynall & McIntosh, 2023).

text.text: Consistent with the DSM-5 guidelines (APA, 2013), more than one thousand unique MDD phenotypes have been identified with individuals commonly endorsing distinct symptom profiles despite sharing the same MDD diagnosis (Fried & Nesse, 2015).

text.text: Network analysis has marked a paradigm shift to mental disorder diagnostic systems (Borsboom, 2008; Cramer et al., 2010).

text.text: Under the network analysis paradigm, MDD is theorised to unfold out of complex interactions among clusters of symptoms (Marman & Rhemtulla, 2022).
text.formatted: Under the network analysis paradigm, MDD is theorised to unfold out of complex interactions among clusters of symptoms <ref type="bibr">(Marman & Rhemtulla, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These networks are visualised structures, represented by nodes (i.e., symptoms) and edges (i.e., relationships between symptoms) which conjoin these nodes (Epskamp et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These networks are visualised structures, represented by nodes (i.e., symptoms) and edges (i.e., relationships between symptoms) which conjoin these nodes <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Edges may be weighted to indicate the strength of association and directed to reflect predictive or causal relationships between nodes (Hevey, 2018).

text.text: While MDD has traditionally been modelled as a latent construct where associations among symptoms occur due to a common cause, according to network analysis, associations instead occur due to direct causal relationships among symptoms (Zachar & Kendler, 2017).

text.text: For example, depressed mood may cause insomnia which then causes impaired concentration.
Once these kinds of relationships become self-sustaining, a stable network structure is "activated" (Cramer et al., 2010a; McNally, 2016).
text.formatted: Once these kinds of relationships become self-sustaining, a stable network structure is "activated" <ref type="bibr">(Cramer et al., 2010a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">McNally, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: While the network approach is not primarily concerned with reclassifying mental disorders, it offers both a theoretical and statistical framework for exploring symptom relationships and how they transition (Eaton et al., 2023).
text.formatted: While the network approach is not primarily concerned with reclassifying mental disorders, it offers both a theoretical and statistical framework for exploring symptom relationships and how they transition <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Eaton et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Numerous properties of network analysis have been argued to provide advantage over latent modelling techniques such as structural equation modelling (SEM; Stein et al., 2017), especially for a MDD research context (Kim & Mackinnon, 2024; Park et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Numerous properties of network analysis have been argued to provide advantage over latent modelling techniques such as structural equation modelling (SEM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Stein et al., 2017)</ref>, especially for a MDD research context <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Kim & Mackinnon, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Park et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Most prominent of these features includes node centrality, which indicates the relative influence of a symptom within a network structure (Epskamp & Fried, 2018).
text.formatted: Most prominent of these features includes node centrality, which indicates the relative influence of a symptom within a network structure <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp & Fried, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Standard centrality measures include: (i) strength, which measures how connected a given symptom is to other symptoms within the same network; (ii) betweenness, which identifies how frequently a symptom appears on the shortest path between other symptoms; (iii) closeness, which is a measure of the shortest path lengths from that symptom to other symptoms; and (iv) expected influence (EI), which was introduced specifically for psychopathological networks by accounting for both positive and negative edge weights (see Robinaugh et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Standard centrality measures include: (i) strength, which measures how connected a given symptom is to other symptoms within the same network; (ii) betweenness, which identifies how frequently a symptom appears on the shortest path between other symptoms; (iii) closeness, which is a measure of the shortest path lengths from that symptom to other symptoms; and (iv) expected influence (EI), which was introduced specifically for psychopathological networks by accounting for both positive and negative edge weights (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Robinaugh et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Symptoms with high strength and EI centrality have been theorised to activate network structures (Boschloo et al., 2015) and cause the recurrence of mental disorders (Robinaugh et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Symptoms with high strength and EI centrality have been theorised to activate network structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Boschloo et al., 2015)</ref> and cause the recurrence of mental disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">(Robinaugh et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: As such, symptoms are more strongly connected to other symptoms, allowing them to propagate more efficiently.

It has been speculated that symptoms with high strength and EI centrality should therefore be considered candidate targets that may prevent the further development of mental disorders (Rodebaugh et al., 2018) including MDD when treated (Castro et al., 2014).
text.formatted: It has been speculated that symptoms with high strength and EI centrality should therefore be considered candidate targets that may prevent the further development of mental disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Rodebaugh et al., 2018)</ref> including MDD when treated <ref type="bibr">(Castro et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A second advantage of the network analysis approach is the detection of community structures (Briganti et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A second advantage of the network analysis approach is the detection of community structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Briganti et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Community structures are clusters of symptoms that are closely interconnected within a network structure, providing further information about the MDD phenotype under investigation.

It is well-established that MDD can vary in presentation, with the DSM-5-TR introducing 'subtypes' and 'specifiers' to account for the inherent complexity in patient experiences of MDD (APA, 2022; Fiorillo et al., 2024), such as the melancholic specifier (e.g., profound anhedonia, early morning awakening, psychomotor changes).

text.text: Though rarely applied within MDD network analysis research (Malgaroli et al., 2021), community detection may provide further information regarding the substructure of MDD.

text.text: Finally, network structures can be directly compared (Van Borkulo et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Finally, network structures can be directly compared <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">(Van Borkulo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Network structures vary in connectivity (also referred to as global strength or density), structural configuration, and patterns of centrality (Epskamp et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Network structures vary in connectivity (also referred to as global strength or density), structural configuration, and patterns of centrality <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The direct comparison of network structures affords insight when exploring differences between groups (e.g., sex differences in depression) and within groups (e.g., changes to a depression network structure following an intervention).
It has been suggested, for example, that depressive symptoms become more variable as network connectivity increases (Kelley et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It has been suggested, for example, that depressive symptoms become more variable as network connectivity increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Kelley et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Capturing such differences between network structures is an opportunity for further inferences for how a person or group experiences changes in depressive symptomatology.
MDD symptom networks are overwhelmingly modelled on cross-sectional data, classically estimated using gaussian graphical models (GGMs) or Ising models (see Hevey (2018) for an overview).
text.formatted: MDD symptom networks are overwhelmingly modelled on cross-sectional data, classically estimated using gaussian graphical models (GGMs) or Ising models (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Hevey (2018)</ref> for an overview).

text.text: While cross-sectional network analyses are often a fundamental starting point, MDD is a dynamic condition unlikely to be comprehensively examined crosssectionally (Fried, 2026).
text.formatted: While cross-sectional network analyses are often a fundamental starting point, MDD is a dynamic condition unlikely to be comprehensively examined crosssectionally <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Fried, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Cross-sectional network analyses are notably limited in (i) the extent to which predictive or causal relationships can be identified between symptoms and (ii) the capacity to detect within-person effects.
Both limitations are especially problematic within psychopathological research for two reasons.
First, the temporal sequencing of symptoms (i.e., the order in which symptoms present) is often not theoretically clear.
For example, does anhedonia precede poor sleep quality, vice-versa, or is this relationship potentially bidirectional?
Second, in certain instances, within-person and between-person effects may show opposite directions (i.e., Simpson's paradox; Kievit et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Second, in certain instances, within-person and between-person effects may show opposite directions (i.e., Simpson's paradox; <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Kievit et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A classic example of this can be seen within medical research: on the group level, exercise is associated with improved cardiovascular health.
Conversely, on the individual level, a heartattack is most likely to occur during periods of exercise (Ebrahimi et al., 2021; Johansson et el., 2022).
text.formatted: Conversely, on the individual level, a heartattack is most likely to occur during periods of exercise <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ebrahimi et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Johansson et el., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The limitations of cross-sectional MDD network analysis generated a drive towards temporal network models based on longitudinal datasets, typically modelled using multilevel vector autoregressive (VAR) analysis or cross-lagged panel networks (CLPN; Wysocki et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The limitations of cross-sectional MDD network analysis generated a drive towards temporal network models based on longitudinal datasets, typically modelled using multilevel vector autoregressive (VAR) analysis or cross-lagged panel networks (CLPN; <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Wysocki et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Within temporal network models, within-person and between-person symptom interactions are mapped across time.

This allows for the inclusion of directed edges (where centrality is typically measured using in-strength and out-strength; Bringmann et al., 2019) and predictive relationships to be established between symptoms (Bringmann et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This allows for the inclusion of directed edges (where centrality is typically measured using in-strength and out-strength; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Bringmann et al., 2019)</ref> and predictive relationships to be established between symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Bringmann et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A critical advantage permitted from this approach includes the uncovering of autoregressive effects (i.e., does a symptom at timepoint one predict itself at timepoint two) and crosslagged effects for each changepoint (i.e., does a symptom at timepoint one predict another symptom at timepoint two).
For instance, fatigue in the morning may predict subsequent fatigue later in the day while depressed mood may precede later feelings of worthlessness.

text.text: There are now several opportunities to expand upon this review.

text.text: With the advent of Meta-analytic Gaussian Network Aggregation (MAGNA; Epskamp et al., 2022), a meta-analysis of MDD network analysis studies is now made possible.
text.formatted: With the advent of Meta-analytic Gaussian Network Aggregation (MAGNA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Epskamp et al., 2022)</ref>, a meta-analysis of MDD network analysis studies is now made possible.

text.text: The current systematic review and meta-analysis addresses these opportunities through the following aims: 1) summarise the characteristics of MDD symptom networks, specifying estimation technique, population of interest, and key reported outcomes; 2) undertake a quality appraisal for the studies included in this review, highlighting any inconsistencies in reporting; and 3) estimate a MAGNA of MDD symptom networks based on available cross-sectional data.
Given that network analysis models are largely exploratory in nature, no a priori hypotheses were made for the current review.
This systematic review and meta-analysis was preregistered on PROSPERO (ID: X).
Studies were systematically searched, screened, and selected for inclusion using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Page, 2021).
text.formatted: Studies were systematically searched, screened, and selected for inclusion using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Page, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Initial studies were identified through bibliographies of previous systematic reviews and the following databases on November 17, 2025: MEDLINE, PsycINFO, EMBASE, and CINAHL.

The following Boolean search terms were used: (network structure OR network model OR network approach OR network analysis OR network analyses) AND (depression OR depressive disorder OR major depressive disorder OR depressive symptom) AND (crosssectional OR longitudinal).
Full searches are provided in the Supplementary Materials Table S1.
text.formatted: Full searches are provided in the Supplementary Materials Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.

text.text: Searchers were updated on October 1, 2026.

To be eligible for inclusion for the systematic review, studies had to meet the following criteria: 1) be a published and original empirical study; 2) include a depression diagnosis or measurement of depressive symptoms; 3) conduct a symptom network analysis of symptoms consistent with the DSM-5 guidelines of MDD; 4) be a peer-reviewed study; 5) be written in English.

Studies were excluded if they: 1) were a review article; 2) did not include at least one network analysis consistent with MDD symptoms; 3) included variables in the network other than symptoms consistent with MDD (e.g., comorbid network models).
Studies were first exported to Covidence and then screened based on study title and abstracts by three reviewers (CS, PLD, EL) independently.
All studies that included a network analysis of depressive symptoms were included at this stage.
There was no restriction based on date of publication.
There was moderate interrater reliability for title and abstract screening (Cohen's Kappa 55 -65%).
Two reviewers (CS, PLD) independently reviewed studies included in full text review (Cohen's Kappa 38%).
Disagreements during both the screening and full-text review stages were resolved through consultation with third reviewer (CM).

The following information was extracted and cross-checked by two reviewers (CS, PLD) independently: 1) authors, year of publication, country, data source and recruitment setting; 2) demographic information, including population type, sample size, mean age, gender split; 3) methodological choices including measure of depressive symptoms, diagnostic criteria, analysis technique, number of models, number of nodes included in each network, and intervention for depression where applicable; 4) reported outcomes including most central symptoms, network stability, network characteristics (e.g., global strength), community structures, node predictability; and 5) open science practices, including whether the article was pre-registered, open access, and if data and code were publicly available.
For studies that included a cross-sectional network analysis, we adapted from the quality assessment criteria developed by Oostendorp et al. (2025).

text.text: Within this quality assessment criteria, studies which include a cross-sectional network analysis are rated with respect to 1) sample and reporting quality; 2) quality of analysis; and 3) open science practices.
Scores range from 0 to 18, where greater scores are indicative of higher quality network analysis practices.
Two reviewers (CS, PLD) independently appraised the quality of the cross-sectional network studies included in the current review.
Disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer (CM).
As temporal network models use time-series data, they have different assumptions (e.g., stationarity) and allow for model fit checking.

While there are currently no established quality assessment tools for temporal network analysis studies, we adapted from Oostendorp et al.'s (2025) guidelines in conjunction with a temporal network tutorial paper by Haslbeck et al. text.text: For the centrality rankings of MDD symptoms, we focused on strength centrality for cross-sectional networks and in-and out-strength for the temporal networks.
Across the studies included in this review, we rank ordered the MDD symptoms in terms of relative centrality to other symptoms within the same network structure.
Further information of this procedure is provided in the Supplementary Materials Files 1 and 2.

To be eligible for inclusion in the meta-analysis, studies had to have either made their dataset openly available for use, provide raw datasets, or summary statistics (i.e., Pearson listwise correlation matrices) upon request.
As the MAGNA framework (Epskamp et al., 2022) can only be estimated on cross-sectional data, only studies that estimated a crosssectional network were considered for analysis.

All statistical analyses were conducted in R software (version 4.5.2: R Core Team, 2024).

The meta-analysis was performed via the psychonetrics package in R software (Epskamp, 2020; Epskamp et al., 2022) and followed the MAGNA framework procedures as described in Epskamp et al. (2022) and Isvoranu et al. (2021).

text.text: Under MAGNA, a pooled network analysis is estimated on raw correlation matrices drawn from individual network studies, weighted by the sample size for each dataset.

Provided the large number of datasets, each varying with respect to sample size and participant characteristics, we estimated a random-effects MAGNA model which accounts for cross-study heterogeneity (pruning set to 0.5 to control for false discovery rate).
Within this MAGNA, we plotted nine nodes to represent each MDD symptom described by the DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022).
We note that while not all studies included in this analysis contained all nine MDD symptoms, full information likelihood estimation in MAGNA can handle missing data.
Conversely, some depression measures used across studies have many items (e.g., the CESD-20; Radloff et al., 1977) to capture a larger spectrum of depressive symptomology.
text.formatted: Conversely, some depression measures used across studies have many items (e.g., the CESD-20; <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Radloff et al., 1977)</ref> to capture a larger spectrum of depressive symptomology.

text.text: In such instances, we collapsed these items onto their corresponding core depressive symptom before generating a correlation matrix from which the MAGNA was estimated.
A further breakdown of this procedure is provided in the Supplementary Materials File 3.
We visualised the random-effects MAGNA model of MDD using the R software package qgraph (Epskamp et al., 2012).
text.formatted: We visualised the random-effects MAGNA model of MDD using the R software package qgraph <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Epskamp et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Here, standard deviations between study correlation matrices were estimated as random-effects via cross-heterogeneity tests whereby greater scores indicate greater differences between correlation matrices.
Consistent with standard network practices (Burger et al., 2023), we estimated strength, EI, betweenness, and closeness centralities for this MAGNA model (Epskamp et al., 2012).

text.text: To identify community clusters nested within the MAGNA, a clique percolation method (CPM) was applied using the CliquePercolation package in R software (Lange, 2021).

text.text: Under this method, the parameter k identifies the number of nodes that can form a community, and I (intensity) establishes the minimum edge-weight required for a node to be included within this community.
Permutation tests were run to identify the optimal k and I values for the MAGNA.
The CPM technique is argued to be preferable to other community detection analyses (i.e., walktrap algorithm; Pons & Latapy, 2005) as nodes can belong to multiple communities simultaneously.

text.text: A total of 118 studies included cross-sectional MDD networks.
Of these studies, 29 estimated cross-sectional networks at two separate time points in an intervention design (k = 14) and a longitudinal study design (k = 16).
Most cross-sectional networks were estimated using GGM (k = 73) and based model selection on the Extended Bayesian Information Criteria (EBIC) (k = 80).
Twenty-three studies estimated temporal MDD networks (k = 23).

The most common temporal network models were cross-lagged panel networks (CLPN) (k = 12), followed by panel and multilevel graphical vector autoregressive (GVAR) models (k = 7) (Aitken et al., 2025; Bringmann et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2026; Mathai et al., 2024; Quinn et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a), dynamic time warp analysis (DTW) (k = 2) (Hebbrecht et al., 2020; van Zelst et al., 2022), dynamic exploratory graph analysis (k = 1) (Pereira et al., 2026), and time-lagged logistic regression model (k = 1) (Savelieva et al., 2021).

text.text: The weighted mean age across studies was 35.27 years (SD = 24.84), with ages ranging from 10 to 90 years old.
Most studies recruited from community samples (k = 113), followed by clinical samples (k = 34) and combined clinical and community samples (k = 6).
Participants reported receiving treatment for depression in 25 studies, most commonly medication (k = 14) and psychotherapy (k = 9).
Most studies were conducted in adult populations (k = 101).

Some studies focused on adults with a diagnosis of MDD or endorsed moderate to severe depressive symptoms (k = 35), middle-aged and older adults (aged 45 and older) (k = 8), older adults only (aged 60 and older) (k = 16), adults with chronic disease or physical health conditions (k = 15), women in the perinatal (k = 12) and menopausal (k = 1) stage, university students (k = 3), and adult samples recruited during the COVID-19 pandemic (k = 7).
Few of these studies included generic adult samples without further inclusion criteria (k = 9).
One study recruited a mixed sample of high school students, university students, and older adults aged 60 and above during COVID-19 (Tao et al., 2023).

text.text: Most studies tested edge-weight accuracy using bootstrapped confidence intervals.
Likewise, with respect to node centrality stability, most studies (k = 110) used case dropping bootstraps and reported correlation-stability coefficients (CS-C).
Of the 75 studies that reported CS-C values for strength centrality, the median CS-C value was 0.62 (IQR = 0.44-0.75), indicating adequate stability.

Only six studies reported CS-C values below the recommended threshold of 0.25 (Bos et al., 2018; Gomez-Cumplido et al., 2024; Izquierdo et al., 2023; Kautzky et al., 2025; Liu & Le, 2025; Shukla et al., 2026).

text.text: Extending Malgaroli et al.'s (2021) review on MDD networks and other MAGNAs of anxiety and PTSD symptom networks (Belli et al., 2026; Isvoranu et al., 2021), this review is the first to apply the MAGNA technique to MDD and the first to examine temporal MDD symptom networks.
text.formatted: Extending <ref type="bibr">Malgaroli et al.'s (2021)</ref> review on MDD networks and other MAGNAs of anxiety and PTSD symptom networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Belli et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Isvoranu et al., 2021)</ref>, this review is the first to apply the MAGNA technique to MDD and the first to examine temporal MDD symptom networks.

text.text: A total of 501 networks across 153 studies were included in the current review.
Three primary findings are worth noting.

First, central symptoms of MDD differed between cross-sectional and temporal networks with depressed mood and fatigue had the highest strength centralities across the 130 cross-sectional MDD network studies.
In contrast, depressed mood and psychomotor agitation had the highest in-strength and out-strength centralities among the 23 studies that examined temporal MDD networks.
Second, MAGNA of cross-sectional studies also highlighted depressed mood as the most central symptoms and indicated that cross-study edge heterogeneity was present.
Third, there was notable variability in methodological designs, including MDD measures, network analysis estimation techniques, and standards of reporting.
A key finding of this review was the difference in symptom centrality between crosssectional and temporal MDD networks.
In cross-sectional networks and consistent with Malgaroli et al. (2021), depressed mood and fatigue emerged with the highest strength centralities in cross-sectional networks.
text.formatted: In cross-sectional networks and consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Malgaroli et al. (2021)</ref>, depressed mood and fatigue emerged with the highest strength centralities in cross-sectional networks.

text.text: In contrast, depressed mood exhibited the highest instrength and out-strength centrality in temporal networks, closely followed by psychomotor agitation for in-strength and insomnia or hypersomnia for out-strength.
Previous studies have identified similar discrepancies between cross-sectional and temporal symptom networks of MDD (Bos et al., 2017) and alcohol use disorder (Conlin et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous studies have identified similar discrepancies between cross-sectional and temporal symptom networks of MDD <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Bos et al., 2017)</ref> and alcohol use disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Conlin et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that cross-sectional and temporal network techniques capture different aspects of psychological disorder presentations and, as such, may serve different purposes.

For instance, cross-sectional networks may be better suited to examine patterns of symptom co-occurrence across individuals, while temporal networks reflect how symptoms within a psychological disorder trigger each other over time (Bos et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For instance, cross-sectional networks may be better suited to examine patterns of symptom co-occurrence across individuals, while temporal networks reflect how symptoms within a psychological disorder trigger each other over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Bos et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Echoing past research, the present findings caution the over-interpretation of cross-sectional MDD networks as representative of temporal changes or causal influences between symptoms and highlight the need for more temporal network models of MDD, particularly in identifying targets for intervention and delineating causal symptom dynamics that maintain MDD (Huang et al., 2023).

text.text: The prominence of depressed mood and fatigue in MDD symptom networks is not surprising.
Depressed mood has been regarded as a hallmark feature of MDD.
Under both the DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) and the ICD-11 (WHO, 2022), either depressed mood or anhedonia is required in order to diagnose a depressive episode.

Similarly, fatigue occurs in more than 90% of patients with MDD and can be a prodrome, a baseline symptom that presents within a major depressive episode, or a residual symptom following successful treatment of depression (Ghanean et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly, fatigue occurs in more than 90% of patients with MDD and can be a prodrome, a baseline symptom that presents within a major depressive episode, or a residual symptom following successful treatment of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Ghanean et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: It should be noted, however, that fatigue in the context of MDD is heterogeneous, complex, and may overlap with the construct of psychomotor agitation depending on the instrument of use (Demyttenaere et al., 2005).

text.text: For instance, in common self-report measures such as the CES-D (Radloff et al., 1977) and the PHQ-9 (Kroenke et al., 2001), items describing fatigue tend to converge on a perceived loss of energy or tiredness, which is congruent with the definition of fatigue in the DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022).

text.text: In contrast, observerrating scales such as the HRDS (Hamilton, 1960) and the MADRS (Montgomery & Åsberg, 1979) assess fatigue as difficulty getting started or slowness in initiating and performing daily activities, which covers both fatigue and psychomotor retardation.

text.text: A factor analysis of depressive symptoms as measured by the Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (both clinician-rated and self-report), HDRS, and the BDI revealed that self-rated items measuring fatigue loaded on a latent "lack of energy" factor, while observer-rated items loaded on a separate "hedonic capacity" factor (Gullion & Rush, 1998).

text.text: Consistent with Malgaroli et al. (2021), in this review, one approach taken to establish central nodes was through rank ordering the MDD symptoms in terms of relative centrality to other symptoms within the same network structure.

text.text: Given the wide array of depression rating scales and differences in symptom coverage between instruments, the distinction in symptom centrality between cross-sectional and temporal MDD networks may not be as pronounced as the data suggests.
Symptoms with high strength centrality are argued to be candidate targets that psychological interventions should be structured around (Xu et al., 2026).

text.text: Building on Malgaroli et al.'s (2021) review of cross-sectional networks, temporal network findings from the present review provide further support for the contribution of depressed mood to the onset, maintenance, and treatment of MDD.

text.text: Evidence also highlights the potential importance of psychomotor agitation, aligning with accruing literature showing that psychomotor agitation can reliably predict treatment response to selective serotonin uptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and electroconvulsive therapy in MDD and bipolar disorder (Di Luch et al., 2026).

text.text: However, these interpretations are tentative, given the small number of studies that investigated temporal MDD networks (k = 23).

Moreover, the clinical utility of a symptom's centrality is still not widely accepted within the literature, owing to a lack of consensus on how to interpret symptom centrality and tailor psychological interventions accordingly (Bringmann et al., 2019; Deblander & Hinne, 2019; Hallquist et al., 2019).

text.text: Partly congruent with the aggregated strength rankings reported above, the current MAGNA indicated that depressed mood had the highest strength centrality.

Depressed mood also shared strong edges with fatigue and suicidal ideation, which aligns with considerable literature showing that depressed mood is a key predictive factor for suicidal ideation (Riera-Serra et al., 2024).

text.text: Complementing the prior and only review of MDD networks by Malgaroli et al. (2021), the application of the MAGNA technique to MDD networks in this review enabled the quantification of edge heterogeneity between studies.

text.text: Based on the randomeffects standard deviations in the current MAGNA, variability in edge strength was apparent among MDD network studies.
Of note, the edge that conjoined anhedonia and feelings of worthlessness had the highest standard deviation, indicating variation in how this edge presents between individual MDD network structures.

Although there has yet to be a threshold for determining low, moderate, and high level of edge heterogeneity at the time of conducting this review, the MAGNA results indicate that the generalisability of individual MDD network analyses should be interpreted with caution.

Stable community structures were not detected in the current MAGNA, contrasting robust community structures that were identified in individual MDD networks (Bos et al., 2018; Hakulinen et al., 2020; Hebbrecht et al., 2020; Kendler et al., 2018; Belvederi Murri et al., 2021).

text.text: Many prior studies that identified communities used measures with higher item counts.
For example, Bos et al. (2018) and Hebbrecht et al. (2020) used the BDI-II, which consists of 21-items.

text.text: As MDD instruments capture a larger spectrum of depressive symptomology, modelling MDD networks based on higher item counts may increase the likelihood that non-trivial communities are formed.
Similar to Malgaroli et al. (2021), there was considerable inconsistency in measurement scales used to derive MDD networks.
text.formatted: Similar to <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Malgaroli et al. (2021)</ref>, there was considerable inconsistency in measurement scales used to derive MDD networks.

text.text: In particular, cross-sectional and temporal networks in the current review were constructed from a total of 23 depression rating scales, including self-report and clinician-rated measures.
The heterogeneity in measures of MDD symptoms poses several concerns regarding the validity of our findings.

First, research suggests that self-report ratings of depressive symptomatology tend to be more severe and identify lower efficacy of depression treatments than observer reports (Levis et al., 2020; Miguel et al., 2025; von Glischinski et al., 2021).

text.text: Second, depression measurement scales often cover different content and have been shown to have weak correlations with one another (Fried et al., 2016; Furukawa et al., 2019; Sayer et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Second, depression measurement scales often cover different content and have been shown to have weak correlations with one another <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Fried et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Furukawa et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Sayer et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: This partly reflects the atheoretical nature of depression scale development and the different purposes for formulating different scales (Fried et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This partly reflects the atheoretical nature of depression scale development and the different purposes for formulating different scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Fried et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The HDRS, for instance, was developed as a benchmark for antidepressant trials in patients already diagnosed with depression and heavily emphasises observations of somatic and behavioural features by the clinician (Hamilton, 1960).
text.formatted: The HDRS, for instance, was developed as a benchmark for antidepressant trials in patients already diagnosed with depression and heavily emphasises observations of somatic and behavioural features by the clinician <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Hamilton, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the BDI primarily captures cognitive and affective symptoms (Beck, 1961).

text.text: Compared to both the HDRS and the BDI, the CES-D focuses on self-report problems that are more common in non-clinical settings, such as feeling lonely or bothered, due to its intended purpose of being a depression screening tool in the general population (Radloff et al., 1977).

text.text: A review of the seven most commonly used depression rating scales, including the CES-D, HDRS, and BDI, found that the scales encompassed 52 distinct MDD symptoms, 40% of which is covered in only one scale (Fried, 2017).

text.text: The potential for self-report ratings to yield different results from observer reports and low symptom overlap among depression scales may have confounded our results on symptom centrality.
Whilst we have attempted to unify measures by mapping their respective items onto the nine DSM-5-TR criteria for MDD (APA, 2022), not all measures neatly corresponded to these symptom domains.

text.text: This aligns with the previous finding that content overlap between the most common depression scales and core MDD symptoms defined by the DSM-5 is only moderate (Fried, 2017).

text.text: Moreover, the DSM-5 has been developed independently of theories and primarily relies on expert and clinical consensus (Kendler & Solomon, 2016).
text.formatted: Moreover, the DSM-5 has been developed independently of theories and primarily relies on expert and clinical consensus <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Kendler & Solomon, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these evidence highlights an urgent need for explicit theories of depression to unify the way we diagnose, monitor, and study depression (Fried, 2017).
text.formatted: Taken together, these evidence highlights an urgent need for explicit theories of depression to unify the way we diagnose, monitor, and study depression <ref type="bibr">(Fried, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Until such objective is achieved, the results of this review should be interpreted with caution.

While the overall standards of reporting were moderate across the included studies, the quality appraisal tools highlighted inconsistency surrounding the handling of missing data and risk of Berkson's Bias for studies investigating clinical samples, potentially biasing the final samples (Ron et al., 2019).

text.text: These findings are consistent with Belli et al.'s (2026) review on symptoms of generalised anxiety disorder.

text.text: Accordingly, future network analysis research should make an effort to recruit more representative samples and handle missing data through the appropriate means (e.g., multiple imputation).
For temporal network analysis studies specifically, very few accounted for uncertainty measures or systematic model checking.

text.text: There are several limitations of the current review.
First, although our review included 117 cross-sectional studies, only 14 studies were included in our MAGNA.
This relatively small number of available datasets prevented MAGNA sub-analyses that could have been clinically relevant.
For example, both Isvoranu et al. (2021) and Belli et al. (2026) compared MAGNAs between clinical and non-clinical samples.
text.formatted: For example, both <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Isvoranu et al. (2021)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Belli et al. (2026) compared</ref> MAGNAs between clinical and non-clinical samples.

text.text: While the MAGNAs of these subgroups were similar, it is unclear if these trends would replicate in an MDD MAGNA as presented in the current review.

Second, our review did not include grey literature or studies not written in English, and many the datasets included in the current MAGNA were recruited from the same cohort (e.g., the CHARLS; Zhao et al., 2014).

text.text: Because these samples were drawn from the same cohort, we cannot rule out the potential of a clustering effect (Jak et al., 2013) that may have inflated certain characteristics of the MAGNA (e.g., edge strength).

text.text: Noting this, we were careful to not violate the assumption of independence by only including each dataset once in our MAGNA.
Third, MAGNA is currently limited in its ability to produce heterogeneity analyses typical of standard meta-analytic approaches (Epskamp et al., 2022; Martinez et al., 2022).

text.text: Within MAGNA, because cross-study heterogeneity is indexed based on pooled correlation matrices as opposed to raw data, conventional moderation analysis using mean age, proportion of females and other clinical features seen in other meta-analyses could not be conducted.

While most studies recruited from community samples, many studies in the current review included participants with formal MDD diagnoses (Bos et al., 2018; Bringmann et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2025) or other medical conditions (Aitken et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025).

text.text: A useful avenue for future research would be to include individual participant data (IPD) and the examination of clinical moderators into MAGNA, when such an analysis is feasible.
A relatively large share of the studies included in this review performed some form of NCT (k = 79), with gender differences in network structure and global strength being a typical comparison.
However, evidence on the relationship between the severity of a disorder and the global strength of a network has been mixed.

Some research demonstrates that network global strength directly corresponds to symptom intensity (Robinaugh et al., 2020; van Borkulo et al., 2015), while other studies demonstrate this relationship is not as linear as presumed (Bos et al., 2018; Deflorin et al., 2025; McElory et al., 2019).

text.text: The data in the current study suggest that the global strength of an MDD network is not necessarily tied to more severe MDD symptomatology, as indicated by a general lack of significant change in global strength post-intervention.
Instead, the global strength of an MDD network may better represent symptom variability (Kelley et al., 2023) or network temperature (Grimes et al., 2025).

text.text: Here, a further integration of psychological interventions and network analysis is a necessary step for refining our understanding of MDD networks and how this relates MDD symptom severity.

While the current review underscores the ascendancy of MDD network analysis research, the past decade has also seen a major increase in comorbid network analyses (Beard et al., 2016; Kaiser et al., 2021; Strathdee et al., 2026).

text.text: Notwithstanding the methodological caveats of the current meta-analytic review, the current findings provide some useful insights for monitoring and treating depressive symptoms.

Network analysis was partly developed as a tool to improve interventions, such that central symptoms can be regarded as key treatment targets (Borsboom & Cramer, 2013; Briganti et al., 2024; Bringmann et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Network analysis was partly developed as a tool to improve interventions, such that central symptoms can be regarded as key treatment targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Borsboom & Cramer, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Briganti et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Bringmann et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the reviewed literature, interventions focusing on depressed mood, fatigue, and psychomotor agitation should be highly effective for treating MDD.
To date, CBT remains the most extensively researched nonpharmacological treatment for depression and one of the most efficacious interventions for depressive symptoms (Cuijpers et al., 2023).
text.formatted: To date, CBT remains the most extensively researched nonpharmacological treatment for depression and one of the most efficacious interventions for depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Cuijpers et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence from network intervention analyses suggests that CBT can have a symptom-specific effect (Scott et al., 2022; Lancee et al., 2022).

text.text: However, as only 14 studies included in the current review were interventional in design, it is still unclear whether interventions could target single symptoms and which interventions demonstrate superior efficacy for treating MDD (Bringmann & Eronen, 2018; Cuijpers et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, as only 14 studies included in the current review were interventional in design, it is still unclear whether interventions could target single symptoms and which interventions demonstrate superior efficacy for treating MDD <ref type="bibr">(Bringmann & Eronen, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Cuijpers et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions that have demonstrated efficacy in reducing MDD include mindfulness-based approaches, relaxation exercises, behavioural activation, or a combination of these strategies and cognitive restructuring in a CBT protocol.

To better evaluate the clinical utility of network analysis, MDD network analyses would optimally be estimated, and psychological interventions are subsequently tailored to the information conveyed from the MDD network's structure.

For instance, researchers might first identify the most central symptoms in an MDD network, and then directly target those symptoms through a symptom-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (Kaiser et al., 2022; Lancee et al., 2022; Scott et al., 2022).

text.text: This will likely provide clarity on the behaviour of an MDD network structures over the course of an intervention.

The current review adds to the field of network analysis through providing the first MAGNA of MDD, highlighting the central role of depressed mood and adding to the growing MAGNA research (Belli et al., 2026; Isvoranu et al., 2021).

text.text: With the development of MDD symptom network analysis research, both cross-sectional and longitudinal in design, this review highlights areas where current literature converges and diverges.

With many areas across MDD network analysis research that remain for improvement, further efforts toward temporal network analysis and adherence to standard network analysis reporting practices are two fruitful directions.
Together, developments within these places may allow for a more unified and clinically actionable research agenda for MDD.
